text.p: The following are the main stories from Monday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Chancellor Helmut Kohl's junior coalition partners, the liberal Free Democrats (FDP), aim for a special law to cut solidarity surcharge on income tax.
- Situation in flood-hit eastern Germany is stable but still threatening.
- Upturn in fortunes of industrial companies takes root, Ifo institute says.
- Optimism rises among small and medium-sized companies in second quarter of 1997, poll says.
HANDELSBLATT
- Finance Ministry admits Germany would get less income from the Bundesbank under European economic and monetary union (EMU).
- Handelsblatt indicator points to stable growth in western Germany in August.
- Finance Minister Theo Waigel rejects calls for special law to cut solidarity surcharge.
- Retailers declare themselves satisfied with first half of an end-of-summer sale.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Interior Minister Manfred Kanther wants to cut down on number of sick days public servants take off work.
- Hamburg set to lose out if Thyssen and Preussag merge their shipbuilding operations.
- Private cable network operators lodge formal complaint with the European Commission over planned alliance in the sector between Bertelsmann, Kirch and Deutsche Telekom .
- Number of passengers on internal German flights rises in first half of 1997.
DIE WELT
- Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) plan to block government's pensions reform plans.
- Employers say 96 percent of applicants will have found an apprenticeship by the end of the year.
- Leading economic institutes predict Waigel will suffer further shortfalls in income from taxes over the next few years.
